ABSTRACT 26

Background 27

Scabies is endemic in many tropical, resource-poor areas, causing significant morbidity. Our 28

understanding of the true burden of scabies in Africa is very limited, and we lack tools to accurately 29

assess its prevalence, given our reliance on highly qualified doctors and microscopy for diagnosis. 30

The primary objective of this study was to assess the accuracy of minimally trained fieldworker 31

diagnosis of scabies, compared to diagnosis by experienced medical doctors. 32

Methodology 33

We trained 62 fieldworkers with a minimum of secondary school education in the diagnosis of 34

scabies (categorized as either clinical or suspected), and in terms of severity, based on lesion 35

count. Immediately after the training, we assessed their knowledge based on written assessments. 36

We also assessed the diagnostic accuracy of a sub-sample of the fieldworkers in the field compared 37

to the reference standard (experienced medical doctors). 193 individuals were assessed for 38

scabies. The sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV were calculated, as well as agreement (kappa 39

coefficients) between medical doctors and between fieldworkers. 40

Results 41

The overall median results in written assessments were around 80%. Of the 193 people assessed 42

for scabies, 27% were classified as having scabies according to the reference standard. The 43

sensitivity of fieldworker diagnosis compared to the reference standard was 95% (95%CI 93 -100), 44

and the specificity was 99% (95%CI 99-100). The sensitivity for severe scabies was lower at 64% 45

(95%CI 51-75), and the mean specificity was 100%. Kappa coefficients were 1.00 between medical 46

doctors and 0.95 between fieldworkers. 47

Conclusions 48

Fieldworkers without medical qualifications were capable of diagnosing scabies to a similar level 49

of accuracy as experienced medical doctors, after a short period of focal training. This may facilitate 50

rapid assessments of scabies prevalence for public health purposes and decisions about MDA 51

implementation in similar settings. 52

Author summary 53

What is already known on this topic 54

Scabies is a disease that causes intense itchiness which can affect people’s wellbeing and ability 55

to attend work or school, and if left untreated it can lead to further, more severe complications. 56

Typically, scabies is diagnosed by specialist medical doctors using microscopy. However, many 57

countries lack these resources and therefore there is a paucity of data on scabies prevalence. 58

What this study adds- 59

In our study, we trained people with no previous medical training in the diagnosis of scabies over 60

a few days through presentations and assessments. We demonstrated that they were able to 61

diagnose scabies to a similar degree of accuracy compared to experienced medical doctors. 62

How this study might affect research, practice or policy- 63

Understanding that minimally trained fieldworkers are able to diagnose scabies to a similar degree 64

of accuracy as medical doctors, may facilitate the collection of data for survey purposes in resource- 65

poor areas, which in turn may promote advocacy for the disease. 66

INTRODUCTION 67

Scabies is an ectoparasitic skin infestation, endemic in many tropical, resource-poor communities 68

(1). Scabies mites cause skin lesions and intense itch that are often associated with secondary 69

bacterial infections (impetigo) that can lead to more severe sequelae, such as severe soft tissue 70

infection, rheumatic fever, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and sepsis (2,3). In addition to the 71

morbidity associated with scabies, it also has negative profound psychosocial and economic 72

impacts that can perpetuate poverty. Furthermore, effective treatment can be difficult to access in 73

rural, lower-middle income settings, meaning that episodes of scabies are often long-lasting and 74

recurrent. 75

Our understanding of the true prevalence of scabies in the African region is extremely limited. A 76

cross-sectional analysis of global scabies prevalence in 2017 reported no available data sources 77

for sub-Saharan Africa and relied on estimates from other continents and the covariate of water 78

source to estimate the burden of scabies in this region (4). A more recent article reported estimates 79

of scabies prevalence in eight African countries, however, the majority of these estimates were 80

based on small-scale studies, and there were no available data from the remaining 46 countries 81

(1). High-quality data collection has been impeded by the limited investment in scabies control 82

programmes and research. Paradoxically, high quality data is needed to encourage investment into 83

scabies disease programmes and to generate data. Therefore, accessible and economic methods 84

of assessing scabies prevalence are needed to further advocate for investment into scabies control 85

programmes. 86

In sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), the most economically disadvantaged communities often live in rural, 87

difficult-to-reach areas (5). Thus, individuals living with scabies often don’t seek care and therefore, 88

the number of cases seen at health facilities is not a reliable indicator of the true scabies burden in 89

the community (1). Therefore, novel diagnostic approaches and tools for assessing scabies in field 90

settings are needed. 91

Currently, there are no point-of-care diagnostic tests for scabies that are appropriate for use in field 92

settings (6,7). Accessibility and availability of these tools would improve our ability to estimate 93

population prevalence; and provide information that could be used for control programme decision 94

making. Confirmation of scabies diagnosis in high-income clinical settings typically requires 95

examination by an experienced doctor and microscopic visualisation of mites on skin scrapings. 96

However, these methods are not feasible in field settings as they require specialised equipment 97

and highly skilled workers. The need for improved diagnostic tools for scabies has been highlighted 98

as a priority for global scabies control as part of the World Health Organization (WHO) 2030 road 99

map for neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) (8,9). To accommodate this, the consensus diagnostic 100

criteria for scabies were developed in 2020 by a panel of experts convened by the International 101

Alliance for the Control of Scabies (2020 IACS criteria), with the goal of promoting standardised 102

case definitions of scabies and more comparable data sets (10,11). The 2020 IACS criteria define 103

scabies cases as either confirmed, clinical or suspected based on the level of diagnostic certainty. 104

Typically, medical doctors are responsible for assessing whether someone has scabies. However, 105

task-shifting, whereby tasks typically performed by a doctor are shifted to healthcare professionals 106

with less specialised positions, can improve access to healthcare in resource-poor areas (12). The 107

same strategy may be applied for scabies prevalence surveys. There have been a few studies 108

assessing the accuracy non-clinician healthcare professional for the diagnosis of scabies in the 109

field following the IACS criteria in south pacific and west African settings. One study evaluated the 110

diagnostic accuracy of four, briefly-trained nurses who examined a cohort of 171 school children 111

using clinical criteria (13). The researchers found the nurses to have high levels of sensitivity and 112

specificity for moderate to severe scabies (94% and 74% respectively), but low sensitivity for mild 113

scabies, when compared to the consensus diagnosis of two expert physicians. In another study, 114

two dermatologists trained five nurses, and screened 135 people for scabies, and found 55% 115

sensitivity and 90% specificity, with again higher levels of sensitivity for moderate and severe cases 116

(14). Finally, a study evaluated the use of a modified, simplified version of the IACS 2020 criteria 117

for mapping and rapidly assessing scabies prevalence (15) in very-high prevalence settings. This 118

modified version had a sensitivity of 82% and specificity of 98% compared to diagnosis using of 119

the full 2020 IACS criteria, with no difference in the pooled prevalence estimates using the two 120

methods. 121

In 2022, a large-scale randomised-controlled trial (BOHEMIA) took place in Mopeia, Mozambique 122

assessing ivermectin mass drug administration (MDA) for malaria vector control and enrolling over 123

20,000 participants (16). A secondary objective of this clinical trial was to assess the impact of 124

ivermectin MDA on the local prevalence of scabies. The fieldworkers who implemented the MDA 125

had a minimum of secondary school education to grade 10. The resources to screen such a large 126

population using medical doctors and microscopy were not available, and therefore we chose to 127

train a sub-group of the same fieldworkers who implemented the MDA in the diagnosis of scabies. 128

If non-medical workers can accurately identify scabies cases, this may facilitate rapid assessments 129

The primary objective of this study was to assess the accuracy of minimally trained fieldworker 132

diagnosis of scabies in terms of positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), 133

sensitivity and specificity, compared to diagnosis by experienced medical doctors. 134

METHODS 136

Study design and setting 137

This study was nested within a trial that took place between March-September 2022 in Mopeia, 138

Mozambique. This district is located in the central north of Mozambique and has a population of 139

around 162,000 (17). To date, there have been no large-scale published studies reporting scabies 140

in Mozambique(18). 141

Training procedures 142

We trained 90 individuals with high-school qualifications for two days. Between 4th-7th February 143

2022, 28 supervisors and 62 fieldworkers were trained in the diagnosis of scabies and infected 144

scabies by JFA, VL and AH. JFA has a background in infectious disease epidemiology and 145

extensive knowledge of scabies pathology. VL and AH are medical doctors with experience working 146

and diagnosing scabies in tropical, scabies-endemic settings. All fieldworkers had completed 147

secondary education up to grade 10, but experience in healthcare settings was not a specified 148

requirement. Fieldworkers were selected from a larger team of study workers based on observed 149

performance in training for other trial activities. The training techniques were based on methods 150

used in previous studies (13,19). Day 1 consisted of 5 hours of presentations and discussion on 151

scabies and infected scabies. Day 2 included a written assessment (assessment 1) followed by a 152

summary and discussion of the answers. The slides and structure of the training was designed and 153

agreed upon amongst the three trainers. The assessment included 50 photo-based case scenarios, 154

where the trainees were required to assess the presence or absence of scabies lesions, quantify 155

Validation of the fieldworkers’ scabies assessment against the MDs 165

An assessment of the diagnostic accuracy of the trained fieldworkers took place during a three- 166

week period in July 2022. Each day, two fieldworkers and the two medical doctors visited 167

households that consented to participate in the study, within clusters that had previously reported 168

high levels of body itch during the enumeration and census visits conducted in preparation for the 169

trial (Figure 1). 170

The hamlet leaders of these communities were asked for verbal consent 1 day prior to our visit and 171

made community members aware of the planned visit. All household members who were present 172

on the day of the visit were screened. Nine fieldworkers were randomly selected to take part in the 173

assessment. For every visit, two fieldworkers and the two medical doctors jointly asked participants 174

questions about body itch within the past 24 hours and contact history (body itch amongst other 175

household members within the past 24 hours). Due to the need for all assessors to understand the 176

local languages, it was not possible to conduct this part of the diagnosis independently. Following 177

the questionnaire, the fieldworkers and medical doctors each independently examined the exposed 178

skin of the participant. If lesions were present, the assessors counted the number of lesions and 179

this was used as an indicator of severity, with 1-2 lesions classified as very mild; 3-10 mild; 11-49 180

Index test and reference standard 183

After the joint questioning about symptoms and contact history, the fieldworkers were instructed to 184

examine the skin sequentially and without any discussion between them. Then the fieldworkers 185

recorded their results independently and blinded to one another into an electronic questionnaire 186

using a mobile tablet device. The index test was the individual classification of each participant as 187

clinical scabies, suspected scabies, or not scabies by the field workers based on the skin 188

assessment, combined with the participants’ response to the joint questioning. 189

The two medical doctors examined each participant independently and blinded to one another and 190

entered their observations in the tablet. They then shared their results privately with another 191

researcher (JFA) and, if there were any disagreements, they discussed the case until they reached 192

a consensus. The clinician’s joint assessment based on the history of body itch at personal and 193

household levels as well as their own clinical observations was used as the reference standard. 194

We have reported all aspects of the study recommended by STARD 2015 (S1 File). 195

Statistical analysis 215

Scores in the written training assessment were presented as a percentage. We assessed whether 216

there were any associations between age, education level, gender and score using a Pearson’s 217

coefficient for age, and a single factor ANOVA test for gender and education level. 218

For the scabies validation assessment, sensitivity, specificity, PPV (positive predictive value) and 219

NPV (negative predictive value) were calculated for the diagnosis of scabies by comparing the 220

index test to the reference standard. For this, “Observer 1” was collectively represented by FW1- 221

3, and “Observer 2”, collectively represented by FW4-9. 222

Two Cohen’s kappa coefficients were calculated in order to assess the inter-rater agreement 223

between medical doctors, and the rate of agreement between fieldworkers (21). 224

We used Excel (version 1808, Microsoft) and RStudio, version 4.1.1, (R Core Team (2022). R: A 225

DISCUSSION 289

- There is a significant gap in knowledge with respect to scabies prevalence in low and middle- 290

income countries, particularly in SSA. Our reliance on highly trained medical doctors and light 291

microscopy for analysis of skin scraping samples means that it is often not feasible to conduct 292

prevalence surveys. Existing research has indicated that nurses or other health professionals are 293

capable of diagnosing scabies with a moderate-high level of accuracy. The results of this study 294

suggest that individuals without any medical training may also be able to screen individuals for 295

scabies with a similar degree of accuracy as medical doctors after a short, focal training. Given the 296

global shortage of healthcare workers and costs associated with more specialized staff, this may 297

provide a cost-effective alternative method of assessing scabies prevalence. 298

- The results of the training assessments showed that fieldworkers with only secondary education 299

were able to achieve high scores after a short period of training. Our results suggested that this is 300

true regardless of sex, age or level of education (beyond secondary school). When evaluating the 301

accuracy of scabies (suspected or clinical) assessments in the field, our results suggested that 302

diagnoses made by minimally trained fieldworkers compared to those by highly qualified medical 303

doctors, were highly sensitive and specific when considering diagnosis of scabies (either suspected 304

or clinical). When considering the assessment of severity, fieldworker assessments were less 305

sensitive, particularly for severe scabies; there was a tendency to falsely assess severe scabies 306

cases as milder. There also appeared to be less agreement between medical doctors and between 307

fieldworkers with respect to grading the severity of disease. The values of diagnostic accuracy were 308

higher than expected and higher than observed in similar studies. This was most likely due to 309

limitations in the choice of reference standard, as detailed below. 310

- 311

- The main limitation of this study was that the reference standard used did not reflect the gold 312

standard and therefore the values are not representative of the true diagnostic accuracy. The gold 313

standard for scabies diagnosis typically involves examination of the full body, often using 314

dermoscopy for magnification of suspected lesions and burrows, and microscopy of skin scrapings 315

CONCLUSIONS 326

Despite the limitations of the study, the results do suggest that minimally trained workers with 327

secondary school education are capable of diagnosing scabies to a similar degree of accuracy to 328

trained medical doctors. Given the paucity of scabies prevalence data at present, and the limited 329

resources available to support data collection, this may provide a valuable tool for rapid assessment 330

of scabies prevalence where more specialized staff are not available. MDA programmes used for 331

parasitic diseases including malaria, lymphatic filariasis or scabies may offer an opportunity for 332

active case detection and monitoring of scabies. Further evaluations would be needed to better 333

understand the true diagnostic accuracy of these assessments, how factors such as prevalence 334

affect accuracy, and the contexts in which they are appropriate. 335
